title: Flood Risk Follows Valleys, Not Grids: Graph Neural Networks for Flash Flood Susceptibility Mapping in Himachal Pradesh with Conformal Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Flash floods are the most destructive natural hazard in Himachal Pradesh (HP), India, causing over 400 fatalities and $1.2 billion in losses in the 2023 monsoon season alone. Existing risk maps treat every pixel independently, ignoring the basic fact that flooding upstream raises risk downstream. We address this with a Graph Neural Network (GraphSAGE) trained on a watershed connectivity graph (460 sub-watersheds, 1,700 directed edges), built from a six-year Sentinel-1 SAR flood inventory (2018-2023, 3,000 events) and 12 environmental variables at 30 m resolution. Four pixel-based ML models (RF, XGBoost, LightGBM, stacking ensemble) serve as baselines. All models are evaluated with leave-one-basin-out spatial cross-validation to avoid the 5-15% AUC inflation of random splits. Conformal prediction produces the first HP susceptibility maps with statistically guaranteed 90% coverage intervals. The GNN achieved AUC = 0.978 +/- 0.017, outperforming the best baseline (AUC = 0.881) and the published HP benchmark (AUC = 0.88). The +0.097 gain confirms that river connectivity carries predictive signal that pixel-based models miss. High-susceptibility zones overlap 1,457 km of highways (including 217 km of the Manali-Leh corridor), 2,759 bridges, and 4 major hydroelectric installations. Conformal intervals achieved 82.9% empirical coverage on the held-out 2023 test set; lower coverage in high-risk zones (45-59%) points to SAR label noise as a target for future work.

title: TwinForge 90/5: Coverage Driven, Residual Calibrated Digital Twins with Certified Gap and Drift Bounds
venue: International journal of intelligent engineering and systems
abstract: Closed-loop autonomy requires sim-to-real validity under coupled conditions spanning environment, agents, sensors, and system timing.TwinForge-90/5 defines a contract for auditable digital twins using interaction-aware scenario coverage, paired gap bounds, and drift reporting.Scenario generation targets feasible interaction triads and mandatory critical motifs under an operational profile that supplies evaluation bins and weights.Simulator calibration uses a multi-fidelity twin augmented with learned Reality Residuals and an Active Realism Tuner that aligns taskrelevant feature statistics under validated SIL/HIL timing parity.Realism evaluation uses Counterfactual Twinning to construct matched real-synthetic pairs and reports match acceptance rates, distance distributions, and covariate balance diagnostics.The Gap & Drift Auditor converts perception, planning, and control KPIs into a unified per-bin risk, computes a Weighted Relative Gap with paired bootstrap confidence bounds, and produces Drift Cards reporting Earth Mover's Distance shift and a conformal risk inflation bound \delta_{0.95}atconfidence 1-\alphawith \alpha=0.05.Experiments on Waymo Open, nuPlan, and Oxford Radar RobotCar satisfy the contract with SIC_3=0.94,criticalmotif coverage =0.97, and WRG=0.036with95% confidence interval 0.0280.045.Factor ontology, binning, feasibletriad rules, critical-motif library, and KPI-to-risk mapping are fixed and included as contract objects to support repeatable gate outcomes.

title: Two ways an AKI prediction model can look better than it is: whole-stay feature leakage and marginal-only coverage, measured in 20,401 ICU patients
abstract: Abstract Background. Machine-learning models for acute kidney injury (AKI) in the intensive care unit (ICU) are increasingly reported with strong discrimination and, more recently, with conformal prediction sets that carry a formal coverage guarantee. Both headline numbers can be produced by a study design that is not wrong in any single step but that answers an easier question than the clinical one. Objective. To measure, on one ICU cohort, how much two common evaluation choices inflate apparent performance: aggregating features over the whole ICU stay, and reporting conformal coverage marginally rather than per class. Methods. We used a public two-hospital ICU dataset and built a landmark cohort of 20,401 patients: features from the first 24 hours only, outcome defined as incident KDIGO stage 1+ AKI arising after hour 24, and patients already meeting AKI criteria by hour 24 excluded. Models were developed at one hospital (n = 10,830, AKI 11.9%) and validated at a second, independent hospital (n = 9,571, AKI 10.2%). We compared six classifiers, applied split, class-conditional and Mondrian conformal prediction, and ran a controlled ablation in which cohort, outcome, model, split and seed were held fixed and only the feature window varied. Results. Under the landmark design the best model (XGBoost) reached an external AUC of 0.735 (95% CI: 0.720–0.751). Re-fitting the identical model on whole-stay features raised this to 0.919, so the feature window alone accounts for +0.188 AUC; a conventional whole-stay analysis of these data reports 0.935. Repeating the ablation at prediction times of 6, 12, 24 and 48 hours found the inflation at every one (+0.179 to +0.250), so it is a property of whole-stay aggregation rather than of a particular landmark. Conformal prediction showed the second inflation. A marginal rule met its target overall, 90.8% coverage, while covering only 14.3% of patients who developed AKI. We prove this is permitted rather than anomalous: a valid marginal 1 − α rule bounds coverage of a class of prevalence π₁ only by max{0, 1 − α/π₁}, here 1.7%, and recovering 90% AKI coverage marginally would require a 99.0% rule. Class-conditional calibration reached 88.4% AKI coverage directly, at a cost of 50.5% two-label sets, and we prove its guarantee is unaffected by the prevalence difference between sites, so the residual shortfall measures within-class shift (≥ 1.6 percentage points in total variation). Internal cross-validation gave AUC 0.802 ± 0.013 against 0.735 externally, a further gap that a single-site study would not have revealed. Conclusion. Neither inflation requires a mistake in any individual step, and both are invisible in the numbers usually reported. A landmark feature window and per-class coverage should be the default for ICU prediction models, and we give the bound that says how much a marginal guarantee is worth for any given event rate.

title: Finite-Sample Conformal Risk Bounds for Joint Value-at-Risk and Expected-Shortfall Forecasting Under Non-Exchangeable Financial Time Series
abstract: Financial tail-risk observations are non-exchangeable: serial dependence and regime shifts make their joint law depend on the time ordering, invalidating the exchangeability that standard conformal guarantees assume, and expected shortfall is not elicitable on its own, so a forecaster cannot be calibrated to it as a quantile is to its coverage. We ask whether a black-box value-at-risk and expected-shortfall forecaster can be calibrated under such dependence while retaining finite-sample guarantees. We tune a single inflation parameter by conformal risk control on a bounded monotone loss that couples value-at-risk breach frequency with breach magnitude normalised by the model’s predicted value-at-risk–expected-shortfall gap; the guarantee is thus for a tail-gap-normalised exceedance-severity surrogate, and its expected-shortfall reading depends on the predicted gap being a sound tail-gap estimate. Under exchangeability, the method gives finite-sample expected-risk control; for dependent data we invoke a non-exchangeable swap-distance bound and add, for separated calibration points, a regime-drift bound with an explicit cumulative β-mixing cost, plus a high-probability realised-path statement and a heavy-tail rate of order D(p−1)/p. Building regimes causally from previous-month FRED-MD vintages across eight exchange rates, a Bitcoin series, and the GIFT-Eval finance domain, the weighted controller attains a 2.51% violation rate and a Fissler–Ziegel score of 0.431 against 0.441 and 0.439 for the strongest conformal baselines—an incremental gain, not significant at the 5% level, that concentrates in turbulent regimes and at matched capital, supporting calibration of a joint frequency-and-normalised-severity budget rather than distribution-free control of the expected-shortfall forecast itself.

title: Robust conformal gaussian process regression for CO2 laser engraving: Distribution-free uncertainty quantification and automated quality gating
CREDO: Epistemic-Aware Conformalized Credal Envelopes for Regression
abstract: Conformal prediction delivers prediction intervals with distribution-free coverage, but its intervals can look overconfident in regions where the model is extrapolating, because standard conformal scores do not explicitly represent epistemic uncertainty. Credal methods, by contrast, make epistemic effects visible by working with sets of plausible predictive distributions, but they are typically model-based and lack calibration guarantees. We introduce CREDO, a simple "credal-then-conformalize" recipe that combines both strengths. CREDO first builds an interpretable credal envelope that widens when local evidence is weak, then applies split conformal calibration on top of this envelope to guarantee marginal coverage without further assumptions. This separation of roles yields prediction intervals that are interpretable: their width can be decomposed into aleatoric noise, epistemic inflation, and a distribution-free calibration slack. We provide a fast implementation based on trimming extreme posterior predictive endpoints, prove validity, and show on benchmark regressions that CREDO maintains target coverage while improving sparsity adaptivity at competitive efficiency.

title: Lag-informed thermal response modeling for uncertainty-aware bridge girder-end displacement anomaly detection: A field case study
abstract: Bridge girder-end displacement (GED) is strongly influenced by nonlinear, multichannel, and delayed thermal effects, which can mask weak structural anomalies and undermine fixed residual thresholds. This study develops an uncertainty-aware anomaly-detection framework that combines lag-informed response prediction, dynamic conformal calibration, and sequential evidence fusion. A squeeze-and-excitation temporal convolutional network (SE-TCN) learns the mapping from historical multichannel temperatures to GED, while the Geometric Mean Optimizer (GMO) jointly selects the lag order and architecture-specific hyperparameters under a strictly separated training-validation protocol. Dynamic conformal prediction then constructs an empirically calibrated, time-adaptive normal-response envelope, while anomaly-aware residual admission mitigates calibration contamination by excluding samples classified as anomalous. A fused sequential conformal evidence detector (FSCE) integrates normalized interval exceedance, smoothed conformal evidence, residual bias, and temporal persistence. The framework is evaluated using the field-monitoring data from a single-tower cable-stayed bridge and nine injected anomaly scenarios involving offset, drift, and thermal-sensitivity degradation. The final predictor achieves an RMSE of 0.0479 mm, a MAPE of 0.1580%, and an R 2 of 0.9924. At a nominal coverage level of 95%, the empirical coverage is 94.83% with a mean interval width of 0.2199 mm. Across the nine anomaly scenarios, Proposed-FSCE yields zero false alarms and F1-scores ranging from 0.7950 to 0.9993. Anomaly-aware updating limits the end-inflation ratio to 1.00-1.08, compared with 2.03-7.66 under unconditional updating. These results support the proposed framework as an empirically calibrated approach to bridge-displacement anomaly detection.

title: Radiation-Preserving Selective Imaging for Pediatric Hip Dysplasia: A Cross-Modal Ultrasound–Xray Policy with Limited Labels
abstract: We study an ultrasound-first, radiation-preserving policy for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) that requests a radiograph only when needed. We (i) pretrain modality-specific encoders (ResNet‑18) with SimSiam on a large unlabelled registry (37{,}186 ultrasound; 19{,}546 radiographs), (ii) freeze the backbones and fit small, measurement-faithful heads on DDH relevant landmarks and measurements (iii) calibrate a one-sided conformal deferral rule on ultrasound predictions that guarantees coverage on a held-out calibration set. Ultrasound heads predict Graf and femoral head coverage; X-ray heads predict acetabular index (AI), center–edge (CE) angle, and IHDI grade . On our held out labeled evaluation set, ultrasound measurement error is modest (e.g., MAE 9.7, coverage MAE 14.0%), while radiographic probes achieve AI and CE MAEs of 7.6 and 8.9, respectively. The calibrated US-only policy is explored across rule families (alpha-only; alpha OR coverage; alpha AND coverage), uncertainty inflation factors, and per-utility trade-offs using decision-curve analysis. Conservative settings yield high coverage (e.g., 0.90 for ) with near-zero US-only rates; permissive settings (e.g., alpha OR coverage at larger deltas) achieve non-zero US-only throughput with expected coverage trade-offs. The result is a simple, reproducible pipeline that turns limited labels into interpretable measurements and tunable selective imaging curves suitable for clinical handoff and future external validation.

title: Accounting for Derivatives : Advanced Hedging under IFRS
abstract:
The derivative practitioner’s expert guide to IFRS 9 application
Accounting for Derivatives explains the likely accounting implications of a proposed transaction on derivatives strategy, in alignment with the IFRS 9 standards. Written by a Big Four advisor, this book shares the author’s insights from working with companies to minimise the earnings volatility impact of hedging with derivatives. This second edition includes new chapters on hedging inflation risk and stock options, with new cases on special hedging situations including hedging components of commodity risk. This new edition also covers the accounting treatment of special derivatives situations, such as raising financing through commodity-linked loans, derivatives on own shares and convertible bonds. Cases are used extensively throughout the book, simulating a specific hedging strategy from its inception to maturity following a common pattern. Coverage includes instruments such as forwards, swaps, cross-currency swaps, and combinations of standard options, plus more complex derivatives like knock-in forwards, KIKO forwards, range accruals, and swaps in arrears.
Under IFRS, derivatives that do not qualify for hedge accounting may significantly increase earnings volatility. Compliant application of hedge accounting requires expertise across both the standards and markets, with an appropriate balance between derivatives expertise and accounting knowledge. This book helps bridge the divide, providing comprehensive IFRS coverage from a practical perspective.

Become familiar with the most common hedging instruments from an IFRS 9 perspective
Examine FX risk and hedging of dividends, earnings, and net assets of foreign subsidies
Learn new standards surrounding the hedge of commodities, equity, inflation, and foreign and domestic liabilities
Challenge the qualification for hedge accounting as the ultimate objective

IFRS 9 is set to replace IAS 39, and many practitioners will need to adjust their accounting policies and hedging strategies to conform to the new standard. Accounting for Derivatives is the only book to cover IFRS 9 specifically for the derivatives practitioner, with expert guidance and practical advice.
